index.html.text:
Subresource Integrity (SRI) Checker & Hash Generator

Two tools for the same protection: generate the integrity="sha384-..." value a <script> or <link> tag needs, or check a page's cross-origin tags for a missing integrity attribute, a missing crossorigin attribute (which quietly disables the check in most browsers), or a hash that no longer matches what the CDN serves today.

Generate a hash

Paste the exact file contents (the script or stylesheet as it will be served) — hashed entirely in your browser, nothing sent anywhere.

Paste content above and click Generate hash.

Check a page

Node.js CLI, no dependencies to install — fetches the page and every cross-origin asset it loads, then hashes what each one currently serves:

node cli/check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and sri.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the page URL you pass and the asset URLs that page itself references; nothing goes through this site.

Paste the JSON from the CLI and click Check.

Report

Common questions

What is Subresource Integrity and why does it matter?

Subresource Integrity (SRI) lets a page declare the exact cryptographic hash a script or stylesheet must have before the browser will run or apply it. Without it, a page that loads a library from a third-party CDN is trusting that CDN completely: if the CDN is compromised, misconfigured, or silently changes what it serves, every site loading that file runs whatever it now contains. An integrity attribute turns that silent trust into a check the browser enforces itself.

Why do I need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Reading another site's response body from browser JavaScript is restricted by CORS, and most pages you would want to check do not opt a script into letting your tab read their full HTML. The CLI has no such restriction — it fetches the page and each cross-origin asset directly, the same way curl or any other HTTP client would, then hands the browser page a JSON report to render. The hash generator above does not have this limitation: it hashes content you paste in, with no fetch involved at all.

Why does an integrity attribute need a crossorigin attribute too?

Per the Fetch spec, a cross-origin request has to opt into CORS mode before the browser is allowed to read enough about the response to verify a hash against it. A crossorigin attribute is what makes that opt-in. Without it, most browsers silently skip the integrity check on a cross-origin tag rather than enforcing it — which is worse than having no integrity attribute at all, because the page looks protected and is not.

What does a hash mismatch finding actually mean?

It means the file this tool just fetched from the declared URL does not match the hash written into the page's integrity attribute. Either the CDN-served file has changed since the tag was written — in which case browsers will now refuse to load it at all, breaking the page for every visitor — or the hash was wrong from the moment it was added. Either way, the fix is to regenerate the hash from the file as it exists right now.

Does a clean report mean the page has no supply-chain risk?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented protection — integrity hashes on cross-origin script and stylesheet tags — not a full security assessment. It does not evaluate same-origin code, inline scripts, iframes, images, fonts, or any other resource type, and it cannot see a risk outside that scope. Treat a clean report as evidence about this one protection, not a determination that the page is secure.

More background: why an integrity attribute with no crossorigin attribute leaves a page unprotected, how this tool compares to srihash.org, or why checking a page's tags by hand misses the two failures that matter most.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific protection — integrity hashes on cross-origin script and stylesheet tags. It is not a full security assessment, does not evaluate inline scripts, iframes, images, fonts, or same-origin code, and cannot see a risk outside that scope. A clean report describes what this check found, not a guarantee the page has no supply-chain risk.

vs-checking-tags-by-hand.html.text:
← SRI Checker & Hash Generator

SRI Checker & Hash Generator vs. checking tags by hand

Reading a page's source for SRI protection is a habit every developer already has -- open view-source or devtools, scan for integrity=. It reliably finds one failure and reliably misses the two that turn out to matter more: a crossorigin pairing gap, and a hash that has quietly gone stale. Both require a real fetch, not a read.

Check a page or generate a hash →

Where a manual read of the tags stops being enough.
What you're trying to findReading the source by handThis checker's CLI
A cross-origin tag with no integrity attribute at all. Works. This is the one gap that is visible directly in the markup. Also finds it, plus the two below in the same pass.
An integrity attribute with no matching crossorigin attribute -- which most browsers silently stop enforcing. Only catches it if you already know to check for the second attribute specifically and don't mistake its presence for enforcement. Flags it explicitly, every time, with an explanation of why the pairing matters.
A declared hash that no longer matches what the CDN currently serves. Cannot be determined from the source alone -- the tag looks identical whether the hash is current or stale. Requires re-fetching the asset. Re-fetches every asset that declares a hash and compares it against what the CDN serves right now.
Auditing a page you did not write, with dozens of third-party tags. Slow and easy to miss one, especially on a page you did not author yourself. One command covers every cross-origin script and stylesheet tag on the page.
Running the same check automatically, before every deploy. Not practical to repeat by hand on every change. Exit-code gateable, so it can run in your own CI on every push.

A manual read is still worth doing for a quick sanity check on one tag you just wrote. It stops being reliable the moment the question is "does this whole page's protection still hold" -- which is exactly the question the crossorigin pairing and the hash-drift check exist to answer, and neither is answerable from the HTML alone.

Common questions

What's wrong with just reading a page's view-source for SRI protection?

View-source finds the one failure that is visible in the markup itself -- a cross-origin script or stylesheet tag with no integrity attribute at all. It cannot find the other two failures this portfolio's own testing turned up as more common: an integrity attribute paired with no crossorigin attribute, and a declared hash that no longer matches what the CDN currently serves. Both require information the source alone does not contain.

Can I tell whether a crossorigin attribute is actually enforced just by looking at it?

No -- the attribute being present in the markup and the browser actually enforcing the pairing are two different facts, and reading the tag only confirms the first. Per the Fetch spec, integrity checking on a cross-origin request requires CORS mode, which the crossorigin attribute opts into; without it, most browsers silently skip the check rather than blocking the resource, so a tag with integrity alone looks identical in source to one that is actually protected. There is no visual difference to eyeball.

How would I know if a declared hash has gone stale, just by reading the tag?

You wouldn't -- the tag's integrity value is whatever was written when someone added it, and reading it tells you only what the page's author believed the file's hash was at that time. Whether that value still matches what the CDN serves today requires re-fetching the asset and re-hashing it, which is a network request a manual read of the HTML cannot perform. A hash that has drifted looks exactly like a correct one in the source.

Is this page making a live comparison against reading source code?

No. This is a static page describing a manual method every developer already has access to -- opening view-source or devtools and reading the tags by eye. It names no competing product or company. The checker's own CLI requests go straight from your machine to the page URL you name and the assets it references, never through this site.

Open the SRI Checker & Hash Generator, read why an integrity attribute with no crossorigin attribute leaves a page unprotected, or see how this compares to srihash.org's hash generator.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, documented protection -- integrity hashes on cross-origin script and stylesheet tags -- from one page fetch. It is not a full security assessment and does not evaluate inline scripts, iframes, images, fonts, or same-origin code. A clean report describes what this one fetch found, not a guarantee the page has no supply-chain risk.

vs-srihash.html.text:
← SRI Checker & Hash Generator

SRI Checker & Hash Generator vs. srihash.org

Different shapes: srihash.org generates one integrity hash from one URL you already chose. This tool generates hashes locally from pasted content -- no URL or fetch required -- and its CLI additionally checks an existing page's cross-origin tags for missing integrity, missing crossorigin, or a hash that has drifted from what the CDN serves now.

Generate a hash or check a page →

srihash.org is a well-known, free, single-purpose SRI hash generator: paste the URL of a script or stylesheet, and it fetches that one resource and returns an integrity="sha384-..." value plus a ready-to-paste tag. It solves exactly the step its name describes -- turning one already-chosen URL into a hash -- and nothing before or after that step.

This tool's hash generator does the same conversion, but from pasted file contents rather than a URL, entirely in your browser with the Web Crypto API and no fetch at all -- which also means it can hash a file that has not been deployed to a public URL yet. Its companion CLI (node cli/check.mjs <url> --json) does a different job srihash.org has no mode for: it fetches a page itself, finds every script and stylesheet tag loaded from a different origin, and reports a tag with no integrity attribute at all, an integrity attribute with no crossorigin attribute, or a declared hash that no longer matches what the CDN currently serves.

What each tool answers.
What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Get the hash for one script or stylesheet URL you already know you want to hash. Either — srihash.org fetches it by URL; this tool's generator hashes pasted content, useful when the file is not yet public.
Find out which cross-origin tags on a page you inherited are missing an integrity attribute entirely. This checker's CLI — srihash.org has no page-crawling mode; you would need to already know which tags to look at.
Catch an integrity attribute that most browsers silently skip enforcing because it has no matching crossorigin attribute. This checker's CLI — srihash.org's output is a single tag you paste in yourself, so it cannot audit one already on the page.
Know whether a hash written months ago still matches what the CDN serves today. This checker's CLI — it re-fetches the asset and compares; srihash.org computes a hash once, for the URL you give it, with no notion of an existing declared value to compare against.
Run the same check unattended in your own CI before a page ships. This checker's CLI, exit-code gateable — srihash.org is an interactive, one-URL-at-a-time web form.

These compose rather than compete. A reasonable habit is this checker's CLI first, to find every cross-origin tag on a page and see which ones lack protection or have drifted, then either tool to (re)generate the hash for the specific file you are fixing.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or srihash.org?

They overlap on one thing -- turning a script or stylesheet into an integrity hash -- and differ in what happens before and after that step. srihash.org is a single-purpose generator: you paste the URL of a resource you have already decided to hash, it fetches that one resource, and it hands back the integrity value and a ready-to-paste tag. This tool's hash generator does the same job from pasted file contents rather than a URL, entirely in your browser, and it also ships a CLI that checks a page you did not write the tags for -- finding every cross-origin script and stylesheet tag, and flagging one with no integrity attribute at all, one with integrity but no crossorigin attribute, or one whose declared hash no longer matches what the CDN currently serves. Use srihash.org when you already know exactly which URL you want hashed. Use this tool's checker when you have inherited a page and need to know which of its cross-origin tags are missing that protection or have drifted out of date.

srihash.org is free too -- what does this add?

Being free is not the difference. srihash.org solves one step well: hand it a URL, get a hash. It has no mode for auditing an existing page's tags, so it cannot tell you that a tag is missing integrity entirely, that an integrity attribute is paired with no crossorigin attribute (which most browsers silently fail to enforce, so the tag looks protected and is not), or that a hash written months ago no longer matches what the CDN serves today. This tool's CLI does all three from one page fetch, exits non-zero on a finding so it can gate a CI run, and its hash generator works from pasted content -- useful for a file that has not been deployed to a public URL yet, which srihash.org's URL-based flow cannot hash at all.

Can srihash.org check an existing page for missing SRI protection?

No -- that is not what it does. srihash.org's job starts after you have already picked one script or stylesheet URL to hash; it has no crawl step and no report format for a whole page's tags. If you inherited a page with a third-party CDN tag and do not know whether it is protected at all, srihash.org gives you no way to find that out -- you would need to already know which tags to look at and hash each one by hand. This tool's CLI does that discovery step first: it fetches the page, finds every cross-origin script and stylesheet tag itself, and reports which ones are missing integrity, missing crossorigin, or hashed against a stale version of the file.

Is this page affiliated with srihash.org?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by srihash.org or its operator. srihash.org is named here only to describe what it is and is not, as a well-known free SRI hash generator. What srihash.org currently does and how it works are described on its own site -- check there for what it covers today.

Open the SRI Checker & Hash Generator to hash your own file or check a page, or read why an integrity attribute with no crossorigin attribute leaves a page unprotected.

It is not a full security assessment and does not evaluate inline scripts, iframes, images, fonts, or same-origin code. A clean report describes what this one fetch found, not a guarantee the page has no supply-chain risk.

why-does-sri-need-the-crossorigin-attrib.text:
Why an integrity attribute needs a crossorigin attribute too

Subresource Integrity lets a page declare the exact hash a cross-origin script or stylesheet must have before a browser will run or apply it. It is easy to add the integrity attribute and stop there, assuming the tag is now protected. In most browsers, it isn't -- not without a second attribute most guides mention only in passing.

Why the browser needs permission to check at all

Reading enough about a cross-origin response to verify a hash against it is itself a CORS-gated operation, under the same Fetch spec that governs Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A plain <script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"> tag does not opt into CORS mode by default -- it is what the spec calls a "no-cors" request. Adding crossorigin="anonymous" (or "use-credentials", for the rare case that needs cookies sent) is what opts the request into CORS mode, which is the mode integrity checking requires.

The two ways to get this half right and still be unprotected

Tag hasWhat actually happens
integrity, no crossoriginMost browsers silently skip the integrity check rather than enforcing it. The page source looks protected; a visitor's browser is not checking anything.
crossorigin, no integrityThe request opts into CORS mode, but there is no hash to check it against -- no protection is configured at all, just a slightly different network request.
Both, correctlyThe browser fetches the resource in CORS mode, hashes what it receives, and refuses to run or apply it if the hash does not match one of the declared values.

Check a whole page automatically

The checker on this site fetches a page you name and every cross-origin script/stylesheet tag it loads, and reports exactly which tags are missing integrity, missing crossorigin, or declare a hash that no longer matches what the CDN currently serves -- plus a standalone hash generator for fixing what it finds. The page-fetching half runs as a Node CLI, since reading another site's full HTML from browser JavaScript is itself restricted by CORS; the hash generator has no such limit, because it only hashes content you paste in.

This is evidence about one specific protection, not a full security assessment -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover.
